title: 07 — Architecture Styles & Domain-Driven Design
html:
07 — Architecture Styles & Domain-Driven Design

The architect's actual job: decide which decisions must be made now (because they're expensive to reverse) and which can be deferred. Everything else is drawing boxes.

1. What "architecture" means, concretely

Definition Useful because
"The decisions that are hard to change later" (Fowler) Focuses effort on one-way doors: data model, service boundaries, sync vs async, tenancy model, auth model, primary datastore
"The set of structures needed to reason about the system" Architecture is communication: if nobody can explain it, it doesn't exist
"Everything that isn't a feature but constrains every feature" Cross-cutting concerns are architecture: security, observability, consistency, deployment

One-way vs two-way doors (Bezos):

  • One-way (decide carefully, write an ADR): programming language, primary database, sync vs event-driven, monolith vs services, multi-tenancy model, public API contract, PII/data residency.
  • Two-way (just pick and move): logging library, DI container, folder structure, CSS framework, which cloud region first, internal class design.

⚠️ The classic failure is treating two-way doors like one-way (analysis paralysis on a logging library) while walking through one-way doors casually (choosing MongoDB for relational data in week one).

1.1 Architecture Decision Records

Every significant decision gets a short file in /docs/adr/NNNN-title:

# ADR-014: Lag portfolio overlap calculations by one business day

## Status
Accepted — 2026-03-11 (supersedes ADR-009)

## Context
Holdings arrive T+1 from the custodian; NAV is available T+0. Calculating overlap
on the same calendar date compares mismatched as-of dates, producing spurious
differences (INC-2291, 2025-11-03).

## Decision
All overlap calculations use `PreviousBusinessDay(today)` as the as-of date.
The lag is surfaced in the UI as an explicit "as of" label.

## Consequences
+ Consistent, explainable numbers; no spurious diffs.
− Users cannot see same-day overlap; intraday requests are rejected with a clear message.
− Requires a business-calendar service (added, see ADR-015).

## Alternatives considered
1. Interpolate missing holdings — rejected, invents data.
2. Show partial results with a warning — rejected, users act on the numbers.

Why this matters more than diagrams: in two years nobody remembers why. Without the why, the next engineer "fixes" the lag and reintroduces the incident.

1.2 The C4 model — the only diagramming convention worth standardising on

Level Audience Shows
1. Context Everyone, incl. business Your system as one box + users + external systems
2. Container Technical stakeholders Deployable units: SPA, API, worker, database, queue
3. Component Developers Major building blocks inside one container
4. Code Rarely drawn Class diagrams — generate, don't hand-draw 
flowchart TB
    U["👤 Portfolio Analyst"] --> SPA["Angular SPA<br/>[Container: TypeScript]"]
    SPA -->|HTTPS/JSON| API["Web API<br/>[Container: ASP.NET Core]"]
    API --> DB[("Operational DB<br/>[Container: SQL Server]")]
    API --> CACHE[("Cache<br/>[Container: Redis]")]
    API -->|enqueue| Q[["Queue<br/>[Container: Service Bus]"]]
    Q --> W["Overlap Worker<br/>[Container: .NET Worker + Python]"]
    W --> DB
    API -->|SignalR| SPA
    API -->|REST| CUST["Custodian API<br/>[External System]"]
    style CUST fill:#999,color:#fff

Rule: one Context diagram and one Container diagram per system, kept current. Component diagrams only for the complex containers. Anything more decays into fiction.

2. The architecture styles, compared

Style Structure Best for Worst for Team shape
Layered (n-tier) UI → BLL → DAL → DB CRUD apps, familiar to everyone Deep domain logic; layers become pass-through Any
Modular monolith One deployable, strict module boundaries Most systems. Best default in 2026 Independent scaling of one hot module 1–5 teams
Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters Domain core + adapters at the edges Testability, multiple delivery mechanisms Simple CRUD (ceremony) Any
Clean / Onion Concentric layers, dependencies inward Long-lived domain-rich systems Small apps; junior teams (misapplied) Any
Microservices Independently deployable services per bounded context Independent scaling/deployment, many teams Small teams, unclear domains, chatty workflows 5+ teams
Event-driven Components communicate via events Decoupling, spiky load, audit/replay Simple request/response, strong consistency needs Any (needs maturity)
CQRS Separate read and write models Very different read/write shapes or loads Simple CRUD (doubles the model count) Any
Event sourcing State = the log of events Audit is the product; temporal queries Most systems — genuinely hard Experienced
Serverless Functions per trigger Spiky/irregular workloads, glue, low ops Steady high throughput, long jobs, cold-start-sensitive Small
Pipes & filters Stages transforming a stream ETL, data processing, media Interactive request/response Data teams
Space-based Replicated in-memory grid Extreme concurrency, low-latency trading Everything else Specialist

2.1 The default recommendation

Start with a modular monolith with clean internal boundaries. It gives you: one deployment, one transaction, one debugger, and — crucially — the option to extract a module into a service later, because the boundary already exists.

You cannot easily go the other way. A premature microservice split with wrong boundaries produces a distributed monolith: all the network complexity, none of the independence.

"If you can't build a well-structured monolith, what makes you think microservices are the answer?" — Simon Brown

3. Layered architecture

┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Presentation (Controllers, SignalR hubs) │  ← HTTP concerns only
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Application (use cases, orchestration)   │  ← transactions, no business rules
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Domain (entities, value objects, rules)  │  ← the actual business
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Infrastructure (EF Core, HTTP clients,   │  ← implements domain interfaces
│  file system, queue, cache)              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

Rules: each layer depends only on the one below (or, in Clean/Onion, all point inward toward the domain). No skipping. No upward references.

⚠️ The failure mode: the anemic pass-through. Controller.Get() calls Service.Get() calls Repository.Get(), each adding a mapping and nothing else. Three files, zero value. If a layer only forwards, delete it. Layers exist to hold something; empty layers are pure cost.

4. Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters and Clean Architecture

flowchart TB
    subgraph Adapters_Driving["Driving adapters (input)"]
        REST[REST controller]
        GRPC[gRPC service]
        CLI[CLI]
        SUB[Queue consumer]
        TEST[Test harness]
    end
    subgraph Core["Application + Domain core"]
        UC["Use cases / application services"]
        DOM["Entities · Value objects · Domain services<br/>Ports defined HERE as interfaces"]
        UC --> DOM
    end
    subgraph Adapters_Driven["Driven adapters (output)"]
        EF[EF Core repository]
        HTTP[Custodian HTTP client]
        BUS[Service Bus publisher]
        CACHE[Redis cache]
    end
    REST --> UC
    GRPC --> UC
    CLI --> UC
    SUB --> UC
    TEST --> UC
    DOM -. "port: IPortfolioRepository" .-> EF
    DOM -. "port: IPricingGateway" .-> HTTP
    DOM -. "port: IEventPublisher" .-> BUS

The single rule that defines it: the core defines the interfaces (ports); the outside implements them (adapters). Dependencies always point inward. Nothing in the domain project references EF Core, ASP.NET, HttpClient, or any SDK.

Project layout in .NET:

src/
  Company.Product.Domain/          # entities, VOs, domain events, port interfaces. NO package refs
  Company.Product.Application/     # use cases, DTOs, validation. refs Domain only
  Company.Product.Infrastructure/  # EF Core, HTTP clients, queue. refs Application + Domain
  Company.Product.Api/             # controllers, DI wiring, middleware. refs all (composition root)
tests/
  Company.Product.Domain.Tests/         # pure, fast, no mocks needed
  Company.Product.Application.Tests/    # use cases with in-memory fakes
  Company.Product.Integration.Tests/    # Testcontainers, real DB

🧪 Enforce it with a test, not a code review:

[Fact]
public void Domain_has_no_dependency_on_infrastructure()
{
    var result = Types.InAssembly(typeof(Portfolio).Assembly)
        .Should().NotHaveDependencyOnAny(
            "Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore", "Microsoft.AspNetCore", "System.Net.Http")
        .GetResult();
    Assert.True(result.IsSuccessful, string.Join(", ", result.FailingTypeNames ?? []));
}

(NetArchTest / ArchUnitNET). Architecture that isn't enforced is a suggestion, and suggestions erode in 6 months.

Benefits: the domain is testable with no infrastructure at all (fast, deterministic tests); swapping SQL Server for Postgres, or REST for gRPC, touches one project; the business rules are readable without framework noise. Costs: more projects, more mapping (domain ↔ persistence ↔ DTO), more indirection. ⚠️ Not worth it for a CRUD admin screen. Apply where the domain has real rules.

5. Domain-Driven Design

5.1 Strategic DDD — where the value is

Concept Meaning
Ubiquitous language One vocabulary shared by code, tests, docs, and business conversation. If the business says "position" and the code says "holding record", you have a translation tax on every conversation forever
Bounded context A boundary within which a model and its language are consistent. "Customer" in Billing ≠ "Customer" in Support — and that's fine; don't build one universal model
Context map How contexts relate: Partnership, Shared Kernel, Customer/Supplier, Conformist, Anti-Corruption Layer, Open Host Service, Published Language, Separate Ways
Core / Supporting / Generic subdomain Core = your competitive advantage (invest, build in-house). Supporting = necessary but not differentiating (build simply). Generic = buy/use SaaS (auth, email, payments)
Domain expert collaboration Event storming, example mapping — the modelling happens with the business, not after a requirements doc

The most valuable single question in system design: "where are the bounded contexts?" Because that's also where your service boundaries, database boundaries, and team boundaries should be. Get it right and everything else is easier; get it wrong and no amount of technology fixes it.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Trading["Trading context"]
        T["Trade, Order, Execution"]
    end
    subgraph Risk["Risk context"]
        R["Position, Exposure, Limit"]
    end
    subgraph Reporting["Reporting context"]
        RP["Holding, Valuation, Overlap"]
    end
    Trading -->|"Published events<br/>(Open Host Service)"| Risk
    Trading -->|events| Reporting
    Risk -->|"ACL translates<br/>vendor model"| VEND["Vendor risk engine<br/>(Conformist otherwise)"]

Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL): a translation layer that keeps a foreign/legacy model out of yours. Every vendor SDK, legacy database, or partner API should be behind one. Without it, their model becomes your model and their changes become your outages.

5.2 Tactical DDD — the building blocks

Block Definition Test for it
Entity Identity that persists through change Two objects with the same field values but different IDs are different things
Value object Defined entirely by its values, immutable Money(100, USD) == Money(100, USD) — interchangeable
Aggregate A cluster of entities/VOs with one aggregate root as the only entry point; a consistency boundary Any invariant spanning two objects means they're in one aggregate
Domain event Something meaningful that happened, past tense TradeApproved, not ApproveTrade
Domain service Logic that doesn't naturally belong to one entity OverlapCalculator taking two portfolios
Repository Collection-like access to aggregate roots only One repository per aggregate, never per table
Factory Complex aggregate creation When the constructor would need 8 parameters and 3 lookups 
// Aggregate root — the ONLY way to modify anything inside it
public sealed class Portfolio           // Entity: identity = PortfolioId
{
    private readonly List<Holding> _holdings = [];
    private readonly List<IDomainEvent> _events = [];

    public PortfolioId Id { get; }
    public IReadOnlyList<Holding> Holdings => _holdings;          // no external mutation
    public IReadOnlyList<IDomainEvent> Events => _events;

    // INVARIANT enforced inside the aggregate boundary:
    // total weight must never exceed 100%
    public void AddHolding(InstrumentId instrument, Weight weight)
    {
        var newTotal = _holdings.Sum(h => h.Weight.Value) + weight.Value;
        if (newTotal > 1.0m)
            throw new DomainException(
                $"Adding {weight} would take portfolio {Id} to {newTotal:P2}, exceeding 100%.");

        _holdings.Add(new Holding(instrument, weight));
        _events.Add(new HoldingAdded(Id, instrument, weight));
    }
}

// Value object — immutable, structural equality, self-validating
public readonly record struct Weight
{
    public decimal Value { get; }
    public Weight(decimal value)
    {
        if (value is < 0 or > 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(value),
            "Weight must be between 0 and 1.");
        Value = value;
    }
    public override string ToString() => Value.ToString("P2");
}

Aggregate design rules (Vernon):

  1. Protect true invariants inside one aggregate. If two things must be consistent at the same instant, they belong together.
  2. Design small aggregates. Large ones cause contention and huge loads. Prefer an aggregate of one entity + value objects.
  3. Reference other aggregates by ID, not by object reference. Order.CustomerId, not Order.Customer. This keeps the boundary real and prevents accidental giant object graphs.
  4. Update one aggregate per transaction. Cross-aggregate consistency is eventual, achieved with domain events. This rule is what makes an aggregate-based design scale — and it's the one people break first.

⚠️ When NOT to do DDD: simple CRUD, reporting/read-only apps, short-lived tools, or when there is no domain expert to talk to. DDD costs real effort; it pays off when the domain has complex, changing rules that the business cares about deeply. Applying tactical DDD without strategic DDD (aggregates and value objects but no bounded contexts or ubiquitous language) is the most common and least useful way to "do DDD".

6. CQRS

Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate the model that changes state from the model that reads it.

flowchart LR
    C[Client] -->|Command| CH[Command handler]
    CH --> AGG[Domain aggregate]
    AGG --> WDB[(Write store<br/>normalised)]
    AGG -->|domain event| PROJ[Projector]
    PROJ --> RDB[(Read store<br/>denormalised)]
    C -->|Query| QH[Query handler]
    QH --> RDB

Levels of CQRS — pick the lowest one that solves your problem:

Level What it means Cost
1. Separate methods ITradeReader / ITradeWriter in the same class/service ~zero. Do this always
2. Separate models Rich domain model for writes; flat DTOs + Dapper/raw SQL for reads Low. The sweet spot for most apps
3. Separate databases Write DB + read replica or a denormalised projection Medium. Adds eventual consistency
4. Event-sourced CQRS Write = event log, read = projections High. Only when you need it

Level 2 in practice (very common in .NET): EF Core with a proper domain model for commands; Dapper with hand-written SQL for queries. Reads don't need change tracking, navigation properties, or the domain model — and hand-written SQL for a complex report is clearer and 10× faster than a LINQ query with six Includes.

When to use CQRS: read and write loads differ by orders of magnitude; read shapes are very different from the write model (dashboards, search, reports); different scaling or consistency requirements. When not to: simple CRUD; a team that will forget to handle the eventual-consistency window in the UI. ⚠️ The UX consequence is real: after a command, the read model may not reflect it yet. Handle it explicitly — return the new state from the command, or use optimistic UI, or poll/subscribe. "Where did my record go?" is the #1 CQRS support ticket.

7. Event-driven architecture & event sourcing

7.1 Event-driven

Style Payload Coupling Use
Event notification "Something happened" + ID Loosest; consumer calls back for details High-volume triggers
Event-carried state transfer Full state snapshot in the event Consumer needs no callback; data duplicated Cross-service reads without sync calls
Event sourcing The events are the state — Audit-critical domains
Command message "Do this" to a specific handler Point-to-point Async work dispatch

Events vs commands — say it precisely: an event is a fact in the past tense with zero or many interested consumers and no expectation of a response (OrderPlaced). A command is an instruction to exactly one handler that can be rejected (PlaceOrder).

Benefits: temporal decoupling (consumer can be down), load levelling (queue absorbs spikes), easy fan-out to new consumers, natural audit trail. Costs: eventual consistency, harder debugging (no single stack trace — you need distributed tracing), duplicate/out-of-order delivery must be handled, schema evolution across producers/consumers, testing needs the whole choreography.

Full mechanics — delivery semantics, outbox, idempotency, ordering, DLQ — in 14_MESSAGING_AND_EVENT_DRIVEN.

7.2 Event sourcing

Store every state change as an immutable event; current state = fold over the events.

Events for Portfolio-42:
  1. PortfolioCreated(owner=A, currency=GBP)
  2. HoldingAdded(AAPL, 0.30)
  3. HoldingAdded(MSFT, 0.25)
  4. HoldingWeightChanged(AAPL, 0.35)
  → current state computed by replay; snapshots every N events for speed

Genuine benefits: complete audit by construction; time travel ("what did we believe on 3 Nov?"); new projections over historical data; natural fit for regulated/financial domains. Genuine costs: ⚠️ schema evolution is forever — you can never change an old event, only add upcasters; queries need projections (you can't SELECT ... WHERE); GDPR erasure conflicts with immutability (crypto-shredding is the usual answer); the whole team must understand it; tooling is thinner.

Recommendation: use event sourcing for the one or two aggregates where audit is the product. Do not event-source the whole system because it sounded elegant. This is the highest regret-rate architecture decision in the industry.

8. Microservices

8.1 When they're justified

Microservices trade local complexity for organisational scalability. You pay in network calls, partial failure, distributed data, and operational overhead. You buy independent deployment and independent scaling per team.

Justified when: multiple teams block each other on one deployment pipeline; parts of the system have wildly different scaling profiles; different components need different tech; you need fault isolation for a critical path; regulatory isolation of data. Not justified by: "it's modern", one team, a greenfield product with unknown boundaries, or wanting to try Kubernetes.

The prerequisites (Fowler's "microservice prerequisites") — if you lack these, don't:

  • Rapid provisioning and automated deployment
  • Comprehensive monitoring and distributed tracing
  • A DevOps culture where the team runs what it builds

8.2 Decomposition

Decompose by bounded context / business capability, never by technical layer. "Order Service", "Pricing Service" — not "Database Service", "Validation Service".

Sizing heuristics: small enough to be rewritten in ~2 weeks; owned by one team ("two-pizza"); one bounded context; a change to one business capability touches one service.

⚠️ The tell that boundaries are wrong: most user stories require changes to 3+ services, or services must be deployed together in a specific order. That's a distributed monolith — strictly worse than a monolith.

8.3 Data — the hard part

Database per service. No shared database, no cross-service joins, no foreign keys across boundaries. Shared database = shared schema = coupled deployments = you don't have microservices.

Then how do you query across services?

Need Solution
Read data owned elsewhere API composition (the caller queries both and joins in memory) or CQRS projection (maintain a local read model fed by events)
Transaction across services Saga — a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions
Consistent event publishing Transactional outbox — write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction, a relay publishes it
Reporting across everything A data warehouse / lakehouse fed by CDC or events. Never by querying production services

Saga — orchestration vs choreography:

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as Order Saga (orchestrator)
    participant P as Payment
    participant I as Inventory
    participant S as Shipping
    O->>P: Authorise payment
    P-->>O: Authorised
    O->>I: Reserve stock
    I-->>O: ✗ Out of stock
    O->>P: COMPENSATE — void authorisation
    O->>O: Mark order failed, notify customer
Orchestration Choreography
Control Central coordinator Each service reacts to events
Visibility ✔ The flow is in one place ✘ Emergent — nobody can see the whole flow
Coupling Orchestrator knows all steps Services only know events
Debug Easier Hard without tracing
Use Complex flows, >3 steps, compensation logic Simple fan-out, 2–3 steps

Recommendation: orchestration for anything with compensation. The "look how decoupled we are" appeal of choreography evaporates the first time you have to answer "why is order 12345 stuck?".

⚠️ Sagas give you atomicity-by-compensation, not isolation. Intermediate states are visible to other readers. You must design for it (pending states, reservations with TTL, semantic locks).

8.4 Cross-cutting concerns in a distributed system

Concern Answer
Service discovery DNS + k8s Service, or Consul/Eureka
Configuration Central config service / k8s ConfigMaps + Secrets
Auth Token at the edge (OIDC), propagate a validated identity; mTLS between services
Resilience Timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads (file 01 §11)
Observability Correlation ID on every request + distributed tracing. Non-negotiable; without it you cannot debug
API gateway AuthN, rate limiting, routing, aggregation
Service mesh mTLS, retries, traffic shifting without app code (Istio/Linkerd) — powerful, and a big operational commitment

9. Multi-tenancy (a one-way door — decide early)

Model Isolation Cost/tenant Noisy neighbour Per-tenant restore Use when
Shared DB, shared schema (TenantId column) Lowest Lowest Highest Hard Many small tenants, SaaS at scale
Shared DB, schema per tenant Medium Low Medium Medium Tens of tenants
Database per tenant High High Low Easy Enterprise, regulated, large tenants
Full stack per tenant Highest Highest None Easy Few, very large or sovereignty-bound tenants

⚠️ With shared schema, one missing WHERE TenantId = @tenant is a cross-tenant data breach. Defend structurally, not by discipline: EF Core global query filters + row-level security in the database + an integration test that asserts every query is filtered.

modelBuilder.Entity<Portfolio>().HasQueryFilter(p => p.TenantId == _tenantContext.TenantId);

10. Choosing an architecture — a decision procedure

flowchart TD
    A[New system] --> B{Is the domain complex<br/>with real business rules?}
    B -->|No, mostly CRUD| C[Layered / vertical slices<br/>+ EF Core. Ship it.]
    B -->|Yes| D[Domain model + hexagonal core]
    D --> E{Multiple teams<br/>blocking each other?}
    E -->|No| F[Modular monolith<br/>with enforced module boundaries]
    E -->|Yes| G{Are bounded contexts<br/>well understood?}
    G -->|No| F
    G -->|Yes| H[Extract services along<br/>context boundaries, one at a time]
    F --> I{Read/write shapes<br/>very different?}
    I -->|Yes| J[Add CQRS level 2]
    I -->|No| K[Single model]
    H --> L{Cross-service transactions?}
    L -->|Yes| M[Saga with orchestration<br/>+ transactional outbox]

Quality attributes drive the choice. Write them down with numbers before drawing anything:

Attribute Ask Architectural consequence
Performance p99 latency target? Caching, denormalisation, colocation
Scalability Peak RPS, growth curve? Stateless services, sharding, queues
Availability SLO? Cost of downtime/hour? Redundancy, multi-AZ/region, degradation
Consistency Can users tolerate stale data, and for how long? Sync vs async, CQRS, saga
Security Data classification, compliance regime? Tenancy, encryption, network isolation, audit
Modifiability What's expected to change most? Put the seam there
Observability Can we debug it in production? Tracing, correlation, structured logs
Cost Budget per month? Serverless vs reserved, storage tiering

These trade off against each other — you cannot maximise all. Naming which two you're optimising, and which you're sacrificing, is the architecture.

11. Evolutionary architecture

  • Fitness functions: automated tests for architectural properties — dependency rules (NetArchTest), performance budgets in CI, bundle size limits, "no service calls more than 3 others", cyclomatic complexity gates.
  • Strangler fig for legacy replacement: façade in front, route capability by capability, delete as it goes dark. Never a big-bang rewrite.
  • Branch by abstraction for in-place refactors: introduce an abstraction over the old implementation, add the new one behind it, flip the flag, delete the old.
  • Expand/contract for schema and API changes (file 02 §5.2).
  • Sacrificial architecture: deliberately build v1 knowing you'll throw it away. Fine — as long as it's a decision, not a surprise.

12. Checklist & interview angles

Architecture review checklist

  • Context and container diagrams exist and are current
  • Bounded contexts named; ubiquitous language documented
  • Every one-way-door decision has an ADR
  • Dependency direction enforced by an automated test
  • Consistency requirements stated per operation (strong vs eventual), and the UX for the eventual ones is designed
  • Failure modes enumerated: what happens when each dependency is slow, down, or returns garbage
  • Data ownership unambiguous — one writer per dataset
  • Scaling axis identified (which component scales, and on what signal)
  • Security boundaries and trust zones drawn
  • Observability designed in: correlation IDs, traces, SLIs
  • Migration/rollback path for the next 2 releases
  • Cost estimate at expected and 10× load

🔍 Interview angles

  • Monolith or microservices for a new product? Modular monolith with clean boundaries; extract when a specific, evidenced pressure appears (team contention, divergent scaling). Justify with the cost of a wrong boundary being much higher than the cost of a later extraction.
  • How do you find service boundaries? Bounded contexts from event storming with domain experts; validate by checking that a typical change touches one context and that data ownership is unambiguous.
  • How do you handle a transaction across services? You don't — saga with compensating actions plus a transactional outbox for reliable publishing; accept lost isolation and design for visible intermediate states.
  • When is event sourcing wrong? Almost always, unless audit/temporal query is the product; the schema-evolution and GDPR costs are permanent.
  • What's a distributed monolith and how do you spot one? Services that must be deployed together, share a database, or require multi-service changes for most stories.
  • How do you keep architecture from eroding? Automated fitness functions, ADRs, and reviewing the dependency graph — not just the code.
